newsitem.title: USA: After wild yr, US yield spread ends where it began.
newsitem.headline: After wild yr, US yield spread ends where it began.

text.p: After a year when the U.S. Treasury market was rattled by a blizzard, a government shutdown, early forecasts for a recession and mid-year forecasts of wage inflation, the two-year to 30-year yield curve spread is ending 1996 where it started.

The yield spread was at 79 basis points when the ball dropped in Times Square a year ago. While interest rates are about a half-point higher, the yield spread will end 1996 nearly unchanged at 75 basis points, barring a surprise in the next 24 hours.

"The world in terms of the (Federal Reserve) has not changed all that much since the beginning of the year," said Marilyn Schaja, money market economist at Donaldson. Lufkin & Jenrette Securities Corp.
"You need confirmation of an economy much stronger or weaker than (market) perceptions for the curve to either narrow or widen from where it is now," she said.
Indeed, most market participants expect the curve to remain steady in the first part of 1997, as players collectively see a Fed keeping interest rates unchanged.

"To widen more than 100 basis points the market needs to believe the Fed is going to be easing and to narrow to 50 basis points or less there has to be expectation of Fed tightening," said Michelle Laughlin, chief U.S. Treasury market strategist at Prudential Securities Inc.
"On balance, most people feel that a yield curve spread of 70 to 90 basis points is consistent with a relatively neutral Fed policy," she added.
While market sentiment toward monetary policy changed during 1996, Laughlin noted that a significant body of opinion expected steady interest rates throughout the year.

Early in 1996, when the market feared a recession and thought the Fed would significantly cut short-term rates, the yield curve steepened to around 135 basis points. But the wide spread was short-lived, as stronger data -- triggered by a 700,000 jump in February non-farm payrolls -- shifted sentiment to a Fed about to embark on a tightening cycle. By early March, the spread was back below 100 basis points, and fell below 80 basis points in late May.

"Apart from that period, the curve has done nothing," said John Ryding, senior economist at Bear Stearns & Co. "Most of the year ... it was marked by parallel shifts in the curve as people were repricing the cost of money."
The two- to 30-year spread did not change much over the last seven months of the year, even though the market went through some very volatile periods, players noted.
"It is hard to say exactly why the curve didn't move a lot," Ryding said. "Stability in the federal funds rate was one factor and real stability on inflationary expectations was another.
"Once the Fed eases, the yield curve will steepen and when the Fed tightens, it will flatten," he said.

Indeed, the yield curve was flatter at the end of 1994 than it is now, with a spread of 20 basis points. At the time, the Fed had raised official rates six times in the year, and 1995 began with expectations of further tightening.
Currently, a number of economists forecast upcoming data to show the economy grew at nearly a 4 percent pace in the fourth quarter, which may prompt the market to again price in a tightening.

As such, analysts see the two-year note jumping to 6.0 percent from its current 5.80 percent, and the 30-year bond rising to 6.75 percent from 6.53 percent. Says Ryding: "The same 75 basis point spread."
